PREFACE

This volume contains practically all that remains of the post-Homeric and pre-academic epic poetry.

I have for the most part established my own text. In the case of Hesiod I have been able to use independent collations of several manuscripts by Dr. W. H. D. Rouse; otherwise I have relied on the critical apparatus of the various editions, especially that of Rzach (1902). The arrangement adopted in this edition, by which the complete and fragmentary poems are restored to the order in which they would probably have appeared had the Hesiodic corpus survived intact, is unusual, but should need no apology; the proper place for the Catalogues (for example), fragmentary as they are, is certainly after the Theogony.

In preparing the text of the Homeric Hymns my chief debt—and it is a considerable one—is to the edition of Allen and Sikes (1904) and to the series of articles in the Journal of Hellenic Studies (vols. xv onwards) by T. W. Allen. To the same scholar and to the

v

PREFACE

I am greatly indebted to the Delegates of the Clarendon Press for permission to use the restorations of the Hymn to Demeter, lines 387–401 and 462–470, printed in the Oxford Text of 1912.

Of the fragments of the Epic Cycle I have included only those that seemed to possess distinct importance or interest, and in doing so have relied mostly upon Kinkel's collection and on the fifth volume of the Oxford Homer (1912).

The texts of the Batrachomyomachia and of the Contest of Homer and Hesiod are those of Baumeister and Flach respectively: wherever I have departed from these, the fact has been noted.

Owing to the circumstances of the present time, I have been prevented from giving the Introduction the full revision I would have wished.

RAMPTON, NR. CAMBRIDGE.
Sept. 9th, 1914

INTRODUCTION

magnetic attraction into the Homeric style and manner of treatment, and became mere echoes of the Homeric voice: in a word, Homer had so completely exhausted the epic genre that after him further efforts were doomed to be merely conventional. Only the rare and exceptional genius of Virgil and Milton could use the Homeric medium without loss of individuality, and this quality none of the later epic poets seem to have possessed. Freedom from the domination of the great tradition could only be found by seeking new subjects, and such freedom was really only illusory, since romantic subjects alone are suitable for epic treatment.

In its third period, therefore, epic poetry shows two divergent tendencies. In Ionia and the islands, the epic poets followed the Homeric tradition, singing of romantic subjects in the now stereotyped heroic style, and showing originality only in their choice of legends hitherto neglected or treated only briefly and imperfectly. In continental Greece,¹ on the other hand, but especially in Boeotia, a new form of epic sprang up, which substituted the practical and matter-of-fact for the romance and pathos of the Ionian School. It dealt in moral and practical maxims, in information on technical subjects useful in daily life—agriculture, astronomy, augury, and the calendar—in matters of religion, and in tracing the genealogies of men. Its attitude is summed up in the words of the Muses to the writer of the Theogony: "We can tell many a feigned tale to look like truth, but we can, when we will, utter the truth" (Theog. 26–27). Such a poetry

¹ That is, in Boeotia, Locris, and Thessaly: elsewhere the movement was forced and unfruitful.

INTRODUCTION

could not be permanently successful, because the subjects it deals with—if susceptible of poetic treatment at all—were certainly not suited for epic treatment, where unity of action, which sustains interest and to which each part must contribute, is absolutely necessary. While, therefore, an epic like the Odyssey is an organism, dramatic in structure, a work such as the Theogony is a merely artificial arrangement of facts, and, at best, a pageant. It is not surprising, therefore, to find that from the very beginning the Boeotian school was forced to season its material with romantic episodes, and that later it tends more and more to revert (as in the Shield of Heracles) to the Homeric tradition.

The Boeotian School

How did the continental school of epic poetry arise? There is little definite material with which to answer this question, but the probability is that there were at least three contributing causes. First, it is likely that before the rise of the Ionian epic there existed in Boeotia a purely popular and indigenous poetry of a crude form: it comprised, we may suppose, versified proverbs and precepts relating to life in general, agricultural maxims, weather-lore, and the like. In this sense Boeotian poetry may be understood to have its roots in maxims similar to our English

"Till May be out, ne'er cast a clout,"

or

"A rainbow in the morning
Is the Shepherd's warning."

xi

INTRODUCTION

Second and third, we may attribute the rise of the new epic to the character of the Boeotian people and, as already noted, to a spirit of rebellion against the old epic. The Boeotians, representing the social class that Hesiod claims as his own, were essentially unromantic; their everyday needs set the general boundaries of their ideals, and as a class they cared little for imaginative fancy, for pathos, or for refined thought in itself. To people of this nature, the Homeric epic would be unacceptable, and the post-Homeric epic, with its formulaic atmosphere, its worn-out and overused diction, and its insincere sentiment, would be utterly repellent. We can imagine, therefore, that among such people a settler of Aeolic origin like Hesiod, who was clearly well acquainted with the Ionian epic tradition, would naturally see that the only outlet for his talents lay in applying epic poetry to new themes that his audience could accept.
Though the poems of the Boeotian school¹ were unanimously attributed to Hesiod right up to the age of Alexandrian criticism, they were clearly neither the work of one man nor even of one period: some, no doubt, were fraudulently assigned to him in order to gain wider circulation; but it is likely that most came to be regarded as his partly because of their general character, and partly because the names of their real authors were lost. One fact about this attribution is remarkable — the deep veneration paid to Hesiod.

¹ The surviving collection of three poems, Works and Days, Theogony, and Shield of Heracles, which are the only ones to have come down to us complete, dates at least from the 4th century AD; the title of the Paris Papyrus (Bibl. Nat. Suppl. Gr. 1099) names only these three works.

INTRODUCTION

Life of Hesiod. Our information about Hesiod comes mainly from references and allusions in the works attributed to him, and to these must be added certain traditions about his death and burial collected from later writers.

Hesiod's father (whose name, through a misreading of Works and Days, line 299 — "to Perses, of divine lineage" twisted into "to Perses, son of Dius" — was thought to have been Dius) was a native of Cyme in Aeolis, where he worked as a seafaring trader and perhaps also as a farmer. Driven away by poverty, he returned to mainland Greece and settled at Ascra, near Thespiae in Boeotia (Works and Days, 636 ff.). Either in Cyme or Ascra, two sons, Hesiod and Perses, were born to him, and after his death they divided the farm between them. Perses, however, who is portrayed as an idler and a spendthrift, obtained and kept the larger share by bribing the corrupt "lords" who held power from Thespiae (Works and Days, 37–39). While his brother squandered his inheritance and ultimately fell into poverty (Works and Days, 34 ff.), Hesiod lived the life of a farmer until, according to the very early tradition preserved by the author of the Theogony (22–23), the Muses encountered him while he was tending sheep on Mt. Helicon and "taught him a glorious song" — almost certainly the Works and Days. The only other personal detail recorded is his victory in a poetry contest at the funeral games of Amphidamas at Chalcis in Euboea, where he won the prize, a tripod, which he dedicated to the Muses of Helicon (Works and Days, 651–9).

Before we proceed to the story of Hesiod's death, it is worth asking how far these "autobiographical" references can be treated as historical fact,

xiii

INTRODUCTION

especially as many critics treat some, or all of them, as spurious. In the first place, attempts have been made to show that "Hesiod" is a significant name and therefore fictitious: it is only necessary to mention Goettling's derivation from the Greek words ἵημι and ὁδός (which would make "Hesiod" mean the "guide" in virtues and technical arts), and to refer to the pitiful attempts in the Etymologicum Magnum (under the entry Ἡσίοδος), to show how prejudiced and lacking even in plausibility such efforts are. It seems certain that "Hesiod" stands as a proper name in the fullest sense. Secondly, Hesiod claims that his father—if not he himself—came from Aeolis and settled in Boeotia. There is fairly definite evidence to warrant our acceptance of this: the dialect of the Works and Days is shown by Rzach¹ to contain distinct Aeolisms apart from those which formed part of the general stock of epic poetry. And that this Aeolic-speaking poet was a Boeotian of Ascra seems even more certain, since the tradition is never once disputed, insignificant though the place was, even before its destruction by the Thespians.

Again, Hesiod's story of his relations with his brother Perses has been treated with scepticism (see Murray, Ancient Greek Literature, pp. 53–54): Perses, it is argued, is clearly a mere dummy, set up to be the target for the poet's exhortations. On such a matter precise evidence is naturally [illegible] . . but all probability is against the . . (1) if the quarrel between the brothers were a fiction, we should expect it to be detailed at length and not noticed allusively and rather obscurely—as we find

¹ Der Dialekt des Hesiodos, p. 464: examples are αἴνημι (Works and Days 683) and ἀρώμεναι (ibid. 22).
xiv

INTRODUCTION

it; (2) as MM. Croiset remark, if the poet needed a lay-figure the ordinary practice was to introduce some mythological person—as, in fact, is done in the Precepts of Chiron. In a word, there is no more [illegible] treating Perses and his quarrel with [illegible] than there would be for treating Cyrnus, the friend of Theognis, as mythical.

Thirdly, there is the passage in the Theogony relating to Hesiod and the Muses. It is surely a mistake to suppose that lines 22–35 all refer to Hesiod: rather, the author of the Theogony tells the story of his own inspiration by the same Muses who once taught Hesiod glorious song. Lines 22–3 are therefore a very early piece of tradition about Hesiod, and though the appearance of the Muses must be treated as a graceful fiction, we find that a writer, later than the Works and Days by perhaps no more than three-quarters of a century, believed in the reality of Hesiod and in his life as a farmer or shepherd.

Lastly, there is the famous story of the poetry contest at Chalcis. In later times the modest version in the Works and Days was elaborated, first by making Homer the opponent whom Hesiod defeated, while a later period exercised its ingenuity in developing the story of the contest into the elaborate form in which it still survives. Finally the contest, in which the two poets competed with hymns to Apollo,¹ was relocated to Delos. These developments certainly need no consideration: are we to say the same

¹ T. W. Allen suggests that the combined Delian and Pythian hymns to Apollo (Homeric Hymns III) may have suggested this version of the story, the Pythian hymn showing strong continental influence.

INTRODUCTION

of the passage in the Works and Days? Critics from Plutarch onward have almost unanimously rejected lines 654–662, on the grounds that Hesiod's Amphidamas is the hero of the Lelantine War between Chalcis and Eretria, whose death may be placed around 705 BC—a date which is obviously too late for the authentic Hesiod. Nevertheless, there is much to be said in defense of the passage. Hesiod's claim in the Works and Days is modest, since he neither pretends to have met Homer, nor to have sung at anything other than an impromptu, local festival, so that the supposed interpolation lacks sufficient motive. And there is nothing in the context to show that Hesiod's Amphidamas is to be identified with the Amphidamas whom Plutarch alone connects with the Lelantine War: the name may have been borne by an earlier Chalcidian, an ancestor, perhaps, of the person to whom Plutarch refers.
The story of Hesiod's death may be told in outline. After the contest at Chalcis, Hesiod went to Delphi, where he was warned that "the fate of death should overtake him in the fair grove of Nemean Zeus." Avoiding Nemea on the Isthmus of Corinth, to which he assumed the oracle referred, Hesiod withdrew to Oenoë in Locris, where he was hosted by Amphiphanes and Ganyctor, sons of a certain Phegeus. This place, however, was also sacred to Nemean Zeus, and the poet, suspected by his hosts of having seduced their sister,¹ was murdered there. His body, cast into the sea, was brought to shore by dolphins and buried at Oenoë (or, according to Plutarch, at Ascra); at a later time his bones were removed to Orchomenus. The whole

¹ She is said to have given birth to the lyric poet Stesichorus.
xvi

INTRODUCTION

The story is full of miraculous elements, and the various authorities disagree on numerous points of detail. The tradition seems, however, to be constant in declaring that Hesiod was murdered and buried at Oenoë, and in this respect it is at least as old as the time of Thucydides. In conclusion it may be worth while to add the graceful epigram of Alcaeus of Messene (Palatine Anthology, vii 55).

[Greek epigram, already translated in the passage below:]

"When in the shady Locrian grove Hesiod lay dead, the Nymphs washed his body with water from their own springs, and heaped high his grave; and thereon the goat-herds sprinkled offerings of milk mingled with yellow-honey: such was the utterance of the nine Muses that he breathed forth, that old man who had tasted of their pure springs."

The Hesiodic Poems. The Hesiodic poems fall into two groups according as they are didactic (technical or gnomic) or genealogical: the first group centers around the Works and Days, the second around the Theogony.
I. The Works and Days. The poem consists of four main sections. (a) After the prelude, which Pausanias failed to find in the ancient copy engraved on lead seen by him on Mt. Helicon, comes a general exhortation to industry. It begins with the

   It is from the second and fourth sections that the
poem takes its name. At first sight such a work
seems to be a miscellany of myths, technical advice,

probably Hesiod used much material of a far older
date, just as Shakespeare used the Gesta Roman-
xviii

INTRODUCTION

dates of rising and setting, and the legends connected with them, and probably showed how these influenced human affairs or might be used as guides. The Precepts of Chiron was a didactic poem made up of moral and practical precepts, resembling the gnomic sections of the Works and Days, addressed by the Centaur Chiron to his pupil Achilles. Even less is known of the poem called the Great Works: the title implies that it was similar in subject to the second section of the Works and Days, but longer. Possible references in Roman writers indicate that among the subjects dealt with were the cultivation of the vine and olive and various herbs. The inclusion of the judgment of Rhadamanthys (fragment 1): "If a man sows evil, he shall reap evil," points to a gnomic element, and the note by Proclus on Works and Days 126 makes it likely that metals were also dealt with. It is therefore possible that another lost poem, the Idaean Dactyls, which dealt with the discovery of metals and their working, was appended to, or even formed part of, the Great Works, just as the Divination by Birds was appended to the Works and Days.

II. The Genealogical Poems. The only complete poem of the genealogical group is the Theogony, which traces from the beginning of things the descent and fortunes of the families of the gods. Like the Works and Days, this poem has no dramatic plot; but its unifying principle is clear and simple. The gods are classified chronologically: as soon as one generation is catalogued, the poet goes on to detail

INTRODUCTION

the offspring of each member of that generation. Exceptions are only made in special cases, such as the Sons of Iapetus (lines 507–616) whose position is explained by their treatment at the hands of Zeus. The chief landmarks in the poem are as follows: after the first 103 lines, which contain at least three distinct preludes, three primeval beings are introduced — Chaos, Earth, and Eros, the last serving here as an indefinite reproductive force. Of these three, Earth produces Heaven, to whom she bears the Titans, the Cyclopes, and the hundred-handed giants. The Titans, oppressed by their father, revolt at the instigation of Earth, under the leadership of Cronos, and as a result Heaven and Earth are separated,¹ and Cronos reigns over the universe. Cronos, knowing that he is destined to be overcome by one of his children, swallows each one of them as they are born, until Zeus, saved by Rhea, grows up and overcomes Cronos in a struggle that is not described. Cronos is forced to vomit up the children he had swallowed, and these together with Zeus divide the universe among themselves, like a human estate. Two events mark the early reign of Zeus: the war with the Titans and the overthrow of Typhoeus. Since Zeus is still reigning, the poet can only go on to give a list of gods born to Zeus by various goddesses. After this he formally bids farewell to the cosmic and Olympian deities and enumerates the sons born of goddesses to mortals. The poem closes with an invocation of the Muses to sing of the "tribe of women."
This conclusion served to link the Theogony to what must have been a distinct poem, the Catalogues of Women. This work was divided into four (Suidas
¹ See note on p. 93.

xxi

INTRODUCTION

says five) books, the last one (or two) of which was known as the Eoiae and may have [been a separate] poem: the curious title will be [discussed later].
The Catalogues proper were a series of genealogies which traced the Hellenic race (or its more important peoples and families) from a common ancestor. The reason why women are so prominent is obvious: since most families and tribes claimed to be descended from a god, the only safe clue to their origin was through the mortal woman beloved by that god; and it has also been pointed out that mother-right still left its traces in northern Greece in historical times.

The following analysis (after Marckscheffel¹) will show the principle of its composition. From Prometheus and Pronoia sprang Deucalion and Pyrrha, the only survivors of the flood, who had a son Hellen (frag. 1), the reputed ancestor of the whole Hellenic race. From the daughters of Deucalion sprang Magnes and Macedon, ancestors of the Magnesians and Macedonians, who are thus represented as cousins to the true Hellenic stock. Hellen had three sons, Dorus, Xuthus and Aeolus, parents of the Dorian, Ionic and Aeolian races, and the offspring of these was then detailed. In one instance a considerable and characteristic section can be traced from extant fragments and notices: Salmoneus, son of Aeolus, had a daughter Tyro who bore to Poseidon two sons, Pelias and Neleus; the latter of these, king of Pylos, refused Heracles purification for the murder of Iphitus, whereupon Heracles attacked and sacked Pylos, killing among the other sons of Neleus Periclymenus, who had the power of changing himself into all manner of shapes.

¹ Hesiodi Fragmenta, pp. 119 f.

INTRODUCTION

From this slaughter, Neleus alone escaped (fragments 13, and 10–12). This summary shows the general organizing principle of the Catalogues: each line appears to have been treated in turn, and the monotony was relieved as much as possible by a brief account of famous adventures connected with any of the individuals mentioned—as in the case of Atalanta and Hippomenes (fragment 14). Similarly, the story of the Argonauts appears from the fragments (37–42) to have been told in some detail.

This tendency to introduce romantic episodes led to an important development. Several poems are attributed to Hesiod, such as [illegible] of Peleus and Thetis, the Descent of [illegible], or the Circuit of the Earth (which must have been connected with the story of Phineus and the Harpies, and thus with the Argonaut legend), which nonetheless seem to have originally belonged to the Catalogues. It is highly probable that these poems were interpolations into the Catalogues, expanded by later poets from more summary notices in the genuine Hesiodic work, and subsequently detached from their contexts and treated as independent compositions. This is definitively known to be true of the Shield of Heracles, the first 53 lines of which belong to the fourth book of the Catalogues, and it almost certainly applies to other episodes as well, such as the Suitors of Helen, the Daughters of Leucippus, and the Marriage of Ceyx, which last Plutarch mentions as "interpolated in the works of Hesiod."

To the Catalogues, as we have said, was appended another work, the Eoiae. The title appears to have

¹ Possibly the division of this poem into two books (see p. 199) is a division belonging solely to this "developed poem," which may have included in its second part a summary of the Tale of Troy.

xxiii

INTRODUCTION

This situation arose in the following way: the Catalogues probably ended (compare Theogony 963 ff.) with some such passage as this: "But now, ye Muses, sing of the tribes of women with whom the Sons of Heaven were joined in love, women pre-eminent above their fellows in beauty, such as was Niobe (?)." Each succeeding heroine was then introduced by the formula meaning "Or such as was . . ." (compare fragments 88, 92, etc.). A large fragment of the Eoiae survives at the beginning of the Shield of Heracles, which may be mentioned here. The "supplement" (lines 57–480) is nominally devoted to a description of the combat between Heracles and Cycnus, but the greater part is taken up with an inferior description of the shield of Heracles, in imitation of the Homeric shield of Achilles (Iliad xviii. 478 ff.). Nothing shows more clearly the collapse of the principles of the Hesiodic school than this ultimate servile dependence upon Homeric models.
   At the close of the Shield, Heracles goes on to Trachis to the house of Ceyx, and this detail suggests that the Marriage of Ceyx may have come immediately after the section on Alcmena in the Eoiae: possibly Halcyone, the wife of Ceyx, was one of the heroines celebrated in the poem, and the original section was "developed" into the Marriage, although what form the poem took is unknown.
   Next to the Eoiae and the poems which appear to have been developed from it, it is natural to place the Great Eoiae. This work, again, as we know from fragments, was a list of heroines who bore children to the gods: from the title we must suppose it to have been much longer than the simple Eoiae, but its
1 Goettling's explanation.

xxiv

INTRODUCTION

extent is unknown. Lehmann, remarking that the heroines are all Boeotian and Thessalian (while the heroines of the [illegible] extend to all parts of the Greek world), [illegible] to have been either a Boeotian or Thessalian.

Two other poems are ascribed to Hesiod. Of these the Aegimius (also ascribed by Athenaeus to Cercops of Miletus), is thought by Valckenaer to deal with the war of Aegimius against the Lapithae and the aid furnished to him by Heracles, and with the history of Aegimius and his sons. Otto Müller suggests that the introduction of Thetis and of Phrixus (fragments 1–2) is to be connected with references to the allies of the Lapithae from Phthiotis and Iolchus, and that the story of Io was incidental to a narrative of Heracles' expedition against Euboea. The remaining poem, the Melampodia, was a work in three books, whose plan it is impossible to recover. Its subject, however, seems to have been the histories of famous seers like Mopsus, Calchas, and Teiresias, and it probably took its name from Melampus, the most famous of them all.

Date of the Hesiodic Poems.—There is no doubt that the Works and Days is the oldest, as it is the most original, of the Hesiodic poems. It seems to be distinctly earlier than the Theogony, which refers to it, apparently, as a poem already renowned. Two considerations help us to fix a relative date for the Works. (1) In diction, dialect and style it is obviously dependent upon Homer, and is therefore considerably later than the Iliad and Odyssey: moreover, as we have seen, it is in revolt against the romantic school, already grown decadent, and while

INTRODUCTION

the digamma is still living, it is obviously growing weak, and is by no means uniformly effective.
(2) On the other hand, while tradition steadily places the Cyclic poets at various dates from 776 B.C. onward, it is equally consistent in regarding Homer and Hesiod as "prehistoric." Herodotus indeed places both poets 400 years before his own time; that is, at around 830–820 B.C., and the evidence stated above points to the middle of the ninth century as the probable date for the Works and Days. The Theogony might tentatively be placed a century later; and the Catalogues and Eoiae are again later, but not greatly later, than the Theogony: the Shield of Heracles may be assigned to the latter half of the seventh century, but there is not enough evidence to show whether the other "developed" poems should be regarded as dating as late as this.

Literary Value of Hesiod.—Quintilian's judgment on Hesiod that "he rarely rises to great heights . . . and to him is given the prize in the middle style of speech" is fair, but is liable to give a wrong impression. Hesiod has nothing that remotely approaches such scenes as that between Priam and Achilles, or the pathos of Andromache's preparations for Hector's return, even as he was falling before the walls of Troy; but in matters that fall within the range of ordinary experience, he rarely fails to rise to the appropriate level. Take, for instance, the description of the Iron Age (Works and Days, 182 ff.) with its catalogue of wrongdoing and violence ever increasing until Aidôs and Nemesis are forced to

Yet it remains true that Hesiod's distinctive claim to a high place in Greek literature lies in the very fact of his freedom from classical form, and his serious, yet childlike, outlook upon his world.

The Ionic School

The Ionic School of Epic poetry was, as we have seen, dominated by the Homeric tradition, and while the style and method of treatment are Homeric, it is natural that the Ionic poets avoided cultivating the ground already worked by Homer, and chose instead to treat legends that lay beyond the scope of the Iliad and Odyssey. It is equally natural that they should have particularly selected various phases of the Troy story that preceded or followed the action of the Iliad and Odyssey. In this way, without any deliberate intention, a body of epic poetry was built up by various writers that covered the whole Trojan story. But the entire range of heroic legend was open to these poets, and other groups of epics grew up dealing particularly with the famous story of Thebes, while others dealt with the beginnings of the world and the wars of heaven. In the end there existed a kind of epic history of the world, as the Greeks knew it, down to the death of Odysseus, when the heroic age ended. In the Alexandrian Age these poems were arranged in chronological order, apparently by Zenodotus of Ephesus, at the beginning

Of all this mass of epic poetry only the scantiest fragments survive; but fortunately Photius has preserved for us an abridgment of the synopsis made of each poem of the "Trojan Cycle" by Proclus, that is, Eutychius Proclus of Sicca.

The pre-Trojan poems of the Cycle may be noted first. The Titanomachy, attributed to both Eumelus of Corinth and Arctinus of Miletus, began with a kind of Theogony that told of the union of Heaven and Earth and of their offspring the Cyclopes and the Hundred-handed Giants. How the poem continued we have no way of knowing, but we may suppose that in character it was not unlike the short account of the Titan War found in the Hesiodic Theogony (617 ff.).

What connection bound the Titanomachy to the Theban Cycle is not clear. This latter group was made up of three poems: the Story of Oedipus, the Thebais, and the Epigoni. Of the Oedipodea practically nothing is known, though on the assurance of Athenaeus (vii. 277 E) that Sophocles followed the Epic Cycle closely in the plots of his plays, we may suppose that in outline the story corresponded closely to the history of Oedipus as it is found in the Oedipus Tyrannus. The Thebais seems to have begun with the origin of the fatal quarrel between Eteocles and Polyneices in the curse called down upon them by their father in his misery. The story was then carried down to the end of the expedition under [illegible] Amphiaraus against Thebes. [illegible] Antimachus of Teos) re-

The Trojan Cycle. — Six epics together with the Iliad and the Odyssey made up the Trojan Cycle: the Cyprian Lays, the Iliad, the Aethiopis, the Little Iliad, the Sack of Troy, the Returns, the Odyssey, and the Telegony.

It has been assumed in the foregoing pages that the poems of the Trojan Cycle are later than the Homeric poems; but, since the opposite view has been held, the reason for this assumption must now be given. (1) Tradition places Homer and the Homeric poems proper back in the ages before recorded history began, and at the same time assigns the purely Cyclic poems to specific authors who are dated from the first Olympiad (776 B.C.) onward. This tradition cannot be purely arbitrary. (2) The Cyclic poets (as we can see from the summaries of Proclus) were careful not to trespass on ground already occupied by Homer. Thus, when we find that in the Returns all the prominent Greek heroes except Odysseus are accounted for, we are compelled to believe that the author of this poem knew the Odyssey and judged it unnecessary to deal fully with that hero's adventures.¹ In a word, the Cyclic poems are "written around" the Iliad and the Odyssey. (3) The [illegible] the Aethiopis is clearly copied from the Thersites of the Iliad: in the same poem Antilochus, slain by Memnon and avenged by Achilles, is obviously modeled on Patroclus. (4) The geographical knowledge of a poem like

the Returns is far wider and more precise than that of the Odyssey. (5) Moreover, in the Cyclic poems epic is clearly degenerating morally—if the expression may be used. The chief greatness of the Iliad lies in the character of the heroes Achilles and Hector rather than in the actual events which take place: in the Cyclic writers, facts rather than character are the objects of interest, and events are so packed together as to leave no space for any exhibition of the interplay of moral forces. All these reasons justify the view that the poems with which we now have to deal were later than the Iliad and Odyssey, and if we must acknowledge the possibility of some conventionality in the received dating, we may feel confident that it is at least approximately correct.

The earliest of the post-Homeric epics of Troy are apparently the Aethiopis and the Sack of Ilium, both attributed to Arctinus of Miletus, who is said to have flourished in the first Olympiad (776 B.C.). He set himself to finish the tale of Troy, which, so far as events were concerned, had been left half-told by Homer, by tracing the course of events after the close of the Iliad. The Aethiopis thus included the coming of the Amazon Penthesilea to help the Trojans after the fall of Hector and her death, the similar arrival and fall of the Aethiopian Memnon, the death of Achilles by the arrow of Paris, and the dispute between Odysseus and Aias for the arms of Achilles. The Sack of Ilium¹ as analyzed by Proclus was very similar to Vergil's version in

Lesches or Lescheos (as Pausanias calls him) of Pyrrha or Mitylene is dated to around 660 BC. In his Little Iliad he undertook to elaborate the Sack as related by Arctinus. His work included the adjudication of the arms of Achilles to Odysseus, the madness of Ajax, the bringing of Philoctetes from Lemnos and his cure, the arrival at the war of Neoptolemus who slays Eurypylus, son of Telephus, the making of the wooden horse, the spying of Odysseus and his theft, along with Diomedes, of the Palladium: the summary concludes with the admission of the wooden horse into Troy by the Trojans. It is known, however (Aristotle, Poetics, xxiii; Pausanias, x, 25-27), that the Little Iliad also contained a description of the Sack of Troy. It is probable that this and other redundant episodes disappeared after the Alexandrian arrangement of the poems in the Cycle, either as the result of some later revision, or merely through disuse. Or Proclus may have thought it unnecessary to give both the accounts by Lesches and Arctinus of the same incident.

The Cyprian Lays, ascribed to Stasinus of Cyprus (but also to Hegesinus of Salamis) was designed to do for the events preceding the action of the Iliad what Arctinus had done for the later phases of the Trojan War. The Cypria begins with the first causes of the war, the purpose of Zeus to relieve the overburdened earth, the apple of discord, the rape of Helen. Then

follow the incidents connected with the gathering of the Achaeans and their ultimate landing in Troy; and the story of the war is detailed up to the quarrel between Achilles and Agamemnon with which the Iliad begins.

These four poems rounded off the story of the Iliad, and it only remained to connect this enlarged version with the Odyssey. This was done by means of the Returns, a poem in five books ascribed to Agias or Hegias of Troezen, which begins where the Sack of Troy ends. It told of the dispute between Agamemnon and Menelaus, the departure from Troy of Menelaus, the fortunes of the lesser heroes, the return and tragic death of Agamemnon, and the vengeance of Orestes on Aegisthus. The story ends with the return home of Menelaus, which brings the general narrative up to the beginning of the Odyssey.

But the Odyssey itself left much untold: what, for example, happened in Ithaca after the slaying of the suitors, and what was the ultimate fate of Odysseus? The answer to these questions was supplied by the Telegony, a poem in two books by Eugammon of Cyrene (flourished 568 BC). It told of the adventures of Odysseus in Thesprotis after the killing of the Suitors, of his return to Ithaca, and his death at the hands of Telegonus, his son by Circe. The epic ended by disposing of the surviving characters in a double marriage, with Telemachus wedding Circe, and Telegonus wedding Penelope.

The end of the Cycle marks also the end of the Heroic Age.

The text discusses the Homeric Hymns, noting that hymns to Pan, Dionysus, Hestia, and Hermes appear to have been composed for use at specific religious festivals rather than for recitations, and that with the possible exception of the Hymn to Ares, none of the hymns in the collection can be considered devotional or liturgical. The Hymn is acknowledged as a very ancient form, though the absence of surviving examples from extreme antiquity is attributed to the lack of literary consciousness in early times. The Hymn to Dionysus, of which only two fragments survive, apparently stood first in the collection. The Hymn to Demeter, known only from a manuscript discovered by Matthiae in Moscow, recounts the abduction of Persephone by Hades, Demeter's grief, her stay at Eleusis, and her revenge through famine, ending with Zeus compelling Persephone's return, though she remains partly a deity of the underworld; in memory of her sorrows Demeter establishes the Eleusinian mysteries, which were originally agrarian in nature. The hymn is described as one of the finest literary works of its kind.

definitely continental; Delos is ignored and Delphi alone is the important centre of Apollo's worship. From this it is clear that the two parts need not be of one date—The first, indeed, is ascribed (Scholiast on Pindar Nem. ii, 2) to Cynaethus of Chios (flourished 504 B.C.), a date which is obviously far too low; general considerations point rather to the eighth century. The second part is not later than 600 B.C.; for (1) the chariot-races at Pytho, which began in 586 B.C., are unknown to the writer of the hymn, (2) the temple built by Trophonius and Agamedes for Apollo (lines 294–299) appears to have been still standing when the hymn was written, and this temple was burned in 548. We may at least be sure that the first part is a work from Chios, and that the second was composed by a continental poet familiar with Delphi.

The Hymn to Hermes differs from the others in its burlesque, quasi-comic character, and it is also the best-known of the Hymns to English readers thanks to Shelley's translation.

After a brief narrative of the birth of Hermes, the author goes on to show how he won a place among the gods. First the newborn child found a tortoise and from its shell fashioned the lyre; next, with great cunning, he stole Apollo's cattle and, when charged with the theft by Apollo, forced that god to appear in an undignified way before the tribunal of Zeus. Zeus seeks to reconcile the two, and Hermes, by the gift of the lyre, wins Apollo's friendship and acquires various privileges: a share in divination, lordship over herds and animals, and the role of messenger from the gods to Hades.

The hymn is difficult to date. Hermes' lyre has seven strings, and the invention of the seven-stringed

The hymn must therefore be later than that date, though Terpander, according to Weir Smyth,¹ may have only modified the scale of the lyre; yet while the burlesque character rules out an early date, this feature is far removed, as Allen and Sikes note, from the silliness of the Battle of the Frogs and Mice, so that a date in the earlier part of the sixth century is most probable.

The Hymn to Aphrodite is not the least remarkable work, from a literary point of view, in the whole collection, exhibiting as it does in a masterly way a divine being as the unwilling victim of an irresistible force. It tells how all creatures, and even the gods themselves, are subject to the will of [illegible] Artemis, Athena, and Hestia; [illegible] pride of power caused her to love a mortal, Anchises; and how the goddess visited the hero upon Mt. Ida. A comparison of this work with the Lay of Demodocus (Odyssey viii, 266 ff.), which is superficially similar, will show how far superior is the former, in which the goddess is but a victim to forces stronger than herself. The lines (247–255) in which Aphrodite tells of her humiliation and grief are especially noteworthy.

There are only general indications of date. The influence of Hesiod is clear, and the hymn has almost certainly been used by the author of the Hymn to Demeter, so that the date must fall between these two periods, and the seventh century seems to be the latest date possible.

Finally there is the Battle of the Frogs and Mice. This work tells the story of the quarrel that arose between the two tribes, and how they fought, until Zeus sent crabs to break up the battle. It is a parody of the martial epic, but has little in it that is truly comic or of literary merit, except perhaps the list of curious weapons taken up by the warriors. The text of the poem is in a chaotic state, and there are many interpolations, some dating to the Byzantine period.

Though popularly attributed to Homer, its real author is said by Suidas to have been Pigres, a Carian, brother of Artemisia, "wife of Mausolus," who distinguished herself at the battle of Salamis. Suidas is confusing the two Artemisias, but he may be right in dating the poem to around 480 B.C.

The Contest of Homer and Hesiod

This curious work, in its present form, dates from the lifetime of Hadrian or shortly after his death, but appears to be based in part on an earlier version by the sophist Alcidamas (c. 400 B.C.). Plutarch (Conviv. Sept. Sap., 40) uses an earlier (or at least shorter) version than the one we possess. The extant Contest, however, has clearly combined with the original document much other poorly integrated material on the life and lineage of Homer, drawing on the same general sources as the Life of Homer. Its scope is as follows: (1) the descent (as variously reported) and relative dates of Homer

Muses of Pieria who give glory through song, come here, tell of Zeus your father and sing his praise. Through him mortal men are famous or unknown, celebrated or forgotten, as great Zeus wills. For he easily makes men strong, and easily brings the strong man low; easily he humbles the proud and raises the obscure, and easily he sets the crooked straight and blasts the proud — Zeus who thunders on high and dwells in the loftiest place. This was the will of Zeus, the loud thunderer, and Hermes, the herald of the gods, put speech in her. Zeus named this woman Pandora, because all the gods who dwell on Olympus each gave her a gift — a curse to men who live by bread.

When he had completed this sheer, inescapable trap, the Father sent the glorious Slayer of Argus, the swift messenger of the gods, to bring her to Epimetheus as a gift. And Epimetheus did not remember what Prometheus had told him — never to accept a gift from Olympian Zeus, but to send it back, in case it should turn out to be something harmful to men. He accepted the gift, and only understood his mistake once the evil was already upon him.

Before this, the races of men had lived on earth free from evils, free from hard labor, and free from the terrible diseases that bring death to men — for in misery men age quickly. But the woman lifted the great lid of the jar with her hands and scattered all these afflictions, bringing sorrow and harm to humanity. Only Hope remained inside, in its unbreakable home beneath the rim of the great jar, and did not fly out through the door; for the lid of the jar stopped her, by the will of Zeus, the cloud-gatherer. But countless plagues now roam among men; the earth is full of evils, and so is the sea. Diseases descend upon men day and night of their own accord, bringing suffering to mortals in silence — for wise Zeus took away their voice. There is no way to escape the will of Zeus.

If you wish, I will sum up another tale for you, skillfully and well; take it to heart within your mind: how gods and mortal men sprang from the same origin.

First of all, the immortals who dwell on Olympus created a golden race of mortal men. These lived in the time of Kronos, when he was king of heaven. They lived like gods, with carefree heart, free from toil and grief; nor did miserable old age come upon them, but with hands and feet forever the same they took delight in feasting, beyond all evils. When they died it was as if they were overcome by sleep; all good things were theirs, for the grain-giving earth bore fruit abundantly and without stint of its own accord, and they lived in ease and peace upon their lands with many good things, rich in flocks, beloved by the blessed gods.

But when this race was covered by the earth, they became pure spirits dwelling on earth, noble, guardians of mortal men — who watch over judgments and wicked deeds, roaming everywhere over the earth, clothed in mist — givers of wealth; and this kingly honor was theirs.

Then those who dwell on Olympus made a second race, much inferior, a silver race, like the golden neither in body nor in spirit. A child was reared for a hundred years under the care of his good mother, a great simpleton, in his own home. But when he came to the full measure of youth and the season of manhood,

Now I will tell a fable for kings, wise as they are themselves.

Thus spoke a hawk to a nightingale of the spangled neck, carrying her high up among the clouds, gripped fast in his talons. She, pierced by his curved talons, wept piteously; but he spoke to her masterfully and said: "What are you crying about, foolish bird? One far stronger than you holds you now. You will go wherever I carry you, songstress that you are, and I will make a meal of you or let you go, as I please. He is a fool who tries to match himself against the stronger; he loses the victory and suffers pain on top of disgrace." So spoke the swift-flying hawk, the long-winged bird.

O Perses, listen to Justice and do not foster Outrage. Outrage is evil for a lowly mortal, and even a man of worth cannot easily bear it, but is weighed down by it once he encounters ruin. The better road to what is right lies on the other side; Justice prevails over Outrage in the end. Only the fool learns this by suffering. For Oath runs swiftly alongside crooked judgments. There is a cry when Justice is dragged away, wherever men who devour bribes lead her and pronounce crooked judgments. She follows, weeping, through the city and the haunts of the people, clothed in mist, bringing harm to those men who drove her out and did not deal her straight.

But those who give straight judgments to strangers and to their own people and do not stray from what is just — their city flourishes and its people prosper within it.

Peace, the nurturer of youth, is throughout the land, and wide-seeing Zeus never ordains painful war against them; nor does famine ever accompany men of straight judgment, nor ruin, and they attend to the works of festivity. The earth bears them much livelihood, and on the mountains the oak bears acorns at its crown and bees in its middle; their woolly sheep are heavy-laden with fleeces; their women bear children who resemble their parents; they flourish continuously with good things; they have no need to sail in ships, for the grain-giving plowland bears them fruit.

But for those who care for evil outrage and cruel deeds, wide-seeing Zeus, the son of Cronus, decrees justice. Often a whole city suffers for one wicked man who sins and devises reckless deeds. Upon them the son of Cronus brings great affliction from heaven, famine and plague together, and the people waste away. Their women do not give birth, and households diminish, by the design of Olympian Zeus; and at another time he destroys their wide army, or their wall, or the son of Cronus wrecks their ships upon the sea.

You kings, take heed of this justice yourselves; for the immortals are near among men and observe all those who grind one another down with crooked judgments, having no regard for the eye of the gods. For thrice ten thousand immortal watchers of Zeus roam over the bountiful earth, guardians of mortal men; they watch over judgments and cruel deeds, clothed in mist, traveling everywhere upon the earth.

She is Justice, a virgin, born of Zeus, honored and revered by the gods who dwell on Olympus. Whenever anyone wrongs her by crooked slander, she sits at once beside Zeus her father, the son of Cronos, and reports the unjust mind of men, so that the people may pay for the crimes of their kings, who with sinister intent deflect justice by pronouncing it crookedly. Keep these things in mind, you kings, you gift-devourers, and put all thought of crooked judgments completely from you.

The man who plots evil for another plots it for himself, and a wicked plan is most wicked for the one who devised it.

The eye of Zeus sees all and understands all, and if he wishes, he observes even this, and does not fail to notice what kind of justice a city upholds within itself. As things stand now, I would not wish to be a just man myself, nor have my son be one — for it is a bad thing to be a just man if the greater justice goes to the one who acts more unjustly. But I do not yet expect Zeus the counselor to bring that about.

O Perses, lay these things to heart, and now listen to justice, and forget violence altogether. For this is the law the son of Cronos established for mankind: whereas fish and beasts and winged birds may eat one another, since there is no justice among them —

There is virgin Justice, the daughter of Zeus, who is honored and revered among the gods who dwell on Olympus. Whenever anyone wounds her with lying slander, she sits beside her father Zeus, son of Cronos, and tells him of men's wicked hearts, until the people pay for the mad folly of their rulers who, with evil intent, pervert judgment and deliver crooked verdicts. Guard against this, you rulers, and make your judgments straight — you who feed on bribes; put crooked judgments entirely out of your minds.

He who does harm to another does harm to himself, and evil schemes hurt the schemer most.

The eye of Zeus, seeing all and understanding all, beholds these things as well, if he so chooses, and does not fail to notice what kind of justice a city upholds. Now therefore, may neither I myself be righteous among men, nor my son — for then it would be a bad thing to be righteous — if indeed the unrighteous are to have the greater advantage. He gave justice to humanity, which proves by far the best thing. For if anyone who knows what is right is willing to speak it openly, far-seeing Zeus grants him prosperity. But whoever willfully swears a false oath in his testimony and wrongs justice and is blinded beyond cure, his descendants are left more obscure thereafter; whereas the descendants of the man who keeps his oath are better in time to come.

To you, great fool Perses, I will speak good counsel.

Vice can be had in abundance and easily: the road to her is smooth and she lives very nearby. But the immortal gods have placed sweat before virtue; the path to her is long and steep and rough at first, yet once you reach the summit, hard though it was, it becomes easy.

That man is best of all who thinks everything through for himself, considering what will be better in the end. He too is good who follows one who speaks well. But whoever neither thinks for himself nor takes to heart what another tells him — that man is worthless.

But you, Perses, of divine stock, always keep my counsel in mind and work, so that Hunger may hate you and august, fair-crowned Demeter may befriend you and fill your barn with livelihood. For Hunger is altogether the companion of the idle man. Gods and men alike resent the one who lives without working, like in spirit to the stingless drones who waste the labor of the bees by eating without working. Let it be your pleasure to keep your work in due measure, so that your barns may be full of seasonable livelihood. From work, men grow rich in flocks and wealthy.

Avoid the month of Lenaion, with its bad days, all of them fit to flay an ox, and the frosts that come upon the earth when Boreas blows, which, breathing across the broad sea from horse-rearing Thrace, stirs it up; and the earth and the forest groan. Many tall oaks and thick firs he brings crashing to the nourishing earth in the mountain glens as he falls upon them, and all the vast forest cries out. The beasts shudder and tuck their tails beneath their haunches — even those whose hide is covered with thick fur. For all their shaggy chests, the cold wind blows through them. It passes through the hide of an ox and does not stop it; it blows through the long-haired goat as well; but through the flocks it cannot pass, because their fleece is thick — the force of Boreas cannot penetrate it. It bends even the old man double. But through the tender-skinned young maiden it does not blow — she who stays indoors close to her dear mother, not yet knowing the works of golden Aphrodite — who, having washed her soft skin and anointed herself with rich olive oil, settles deep inside the house on a winter's day, when the boneless creature gnaws its own foot in its fireless home and its wretched haunts. Nor does the sun show her a pasture to make for.

When Orion and Sirius come to the middle of the sky, and rosy-fingered Dawn looks upon Arcturus, then, Perses, gather all the grape clusters and bring them home. Show them to the sun for ten days and ten nights, then cover them in shade for five, and on the sixth draw off into vessels the gifts of much-rejoicing Dionysus. But when the Pleiades and Hyades and the strength of Orion set, then remember that the time for plowing has come; the season is right and the ground awaits.

If desire for stormy seafaring seizes you, when the Pleiades, fleeing the mighty strength of Orion, plunge into the misty sea, then the blasts of every kind of wind blow fiercely. At that time keep your ships no longer on the wine-dark sea, but remember to work the land, as I urge you. Drag your ship onto land and pack it all around with stones, so they may hold back the force of the moist winds; draw out the bilge-plug so that the rain of Zeus does not rot the vessel. Store all the tackle and fittings neatly in your house, folding the wings of the sea-going ship. Hang the well-made rudder above the smoke. And wait yourself for the sailing season until it comes; then drag your swift ship down to the sea, and load a fitting cargo in her, so that you may bring home profit — just as our father and yours, great foolish Perses, used to sail in ships, in want of a good livelihood; and he once came here too, having crossed a great stretch of sea, leaving Aeolian Cyme in a black ship — not fleeing wealth or riches or prosperity,

but wretched poverty, which Zeus gives to men. He settled near Helicon in a miserable village, Ascra, harsh in winter, oppressive in summer, and never pleasant.

And you, Perses, remember to attend to all work in its season, but especially seafaring. Praise a small ship, but put your cargo in a large one; the greater the cargo, the greater the profit, if only the winds hold back their evil blasts.

When you turn your foolish heart to trade and wish to escape from debt and joyless hunger, I will show you the measures of the loud-roaring sea — though I am no expert in seafaring or in ships. For I have never yet sailed the broad sea on a ship, except across to Euboea from Aulis, where the Achaeans once waited out a great storm and gathered their host from holy Hellas to go to Troy, land of beautiful women. There I crossed over to Chalcis for the games of the great-hearted Amphidamas; and the sons of that bold man had proclaimed many prizes. There, I claim, I won the victory with a song and carried off a handled tripod. This I dedicated to the Muses of Helicon, where they first set me on the path of clear song. Such is the whole of my experience with well-riveted ships; yet even so I will tell you the mind of Zeus who holds the aegis, for the Muses have taught me to sing a boundless song.

Fifty days after the solstice, when the season of weary summer comes to its end, the time is ripe for mortal men to sail; you would not wreck your ship, nor would the sea destroy your crew,

— if indeed Poseidon the Earth-Shaker is not unwilling, or Zeus, king of the immortals, minded to destroy them; for the end of good and evil alike rests with those gods. At that season the winds are steady and the sea is harmless: then trust the winds confidently and drag your swift ship down to the sea, and stow all your cargo aboard; make haste to return home as quickly as you can, and do not wait for the new wine and the autumn rain and the oncoming winter and the fierce blasts of the South Wind, which stirs up the sea in company with the heavy autumn rains of Zeus and makes the sea treacherous.

There is another sailing season for men in spring: when, for the first time, leaves on the topmost branch of the fig tree appear no larger than the footprint a crow leaves behind, then the sea is passable and this is the spring sailing. I do not praise it myself; it does not please my heart. It is a snatched voyage — you would have trouble escaping harm. Yet even so men do these things in their foolishness of mind, for wealth is life itself to poor mortals. But it is a terrible thing to die among the waves. No — I urge you to take all these things to heart as I tell you. Do not put all your livelihood into hollow ships; leave the greater part behind and ship only the lesser portion. For it is terrible to meet disaster among the waves of the sea; terrible too if you load an excessive weight onto a wagon and break the axle, and the cargo is ruined. Observe due measure; and timing is best in all things.

For he had learned from Earth and starry Heaven that he was destined to be overcome by his own son, strong though he was, through the scheming of great Zeus. Therefore he kept no blind watch, but was vigilant and swallowed down his children; and unceasing grief seized Rhea. But when she was about to bear Zeus, the father of gods and men, she besought her own dear parents, Earth and starry Heaven, to devise some plan with her so that the birth of her dear child might be concealed, and that retribution might come upon crafty Cronos for his own fate.

Then, wrapping a great stone in swaddling clothes, she gave it to the great lord, son of Heaven, the former king of the gods. He took it in his hands and thrust it down into his belly, the wretch — nor did he perceive in his heart that in place of the stone his own invincible and untroubled son remained behind, who was soon to overcome him by force and strength and drive him from his honor, and reign among the immortals.

Then swiftly the strength and the glorious limbs of the young lord grew, and as the years came round, great Cronos of crooked counsel, beguiled by the cunning advice of Gaia, brought up his offspring again — overcome by the arts and strength of his own son. First he vomited up the stone, which he had swallowed last; and Zeus set it firm in the wide-pathed earth at holy Pytho under the glens of Parnassus, to be a sign thenceforth and a marvel to mortal men.

He freed the paternal uncles of Ouranos from their ruinous bonds — those whom their father had bound in his foolishness. They, in gratitude for his kindnesses, gave him thunder and the blazing thunderbolt and lightning, which monstrous Earth had kept hidden before. Trusting in these, he rules over mortals and immortals.

For when the gods and mortal men came to a settlement at Mekone, Prometheus then divided a great ox with willing spirit and set it before them, meaning to deceive the mind of Zeus. For the one portion he placed the flesh and the rich inner parts covered with fat, laying them within the hide wrapped in the ox's stomach; for the other he arranged the white bones of the ox with clever trickery and covered them with gleaming fat.

Then the father of men and gods addressed him: "Son of Iapetos, most renowned of all lords, good friend, how unevenly you have divided the portions."

So spoke Zeus, who knows immortal counsels, mocking him. But Prometheus of crooked counsel answered him with a gentle smile, not forgetting his cunning craft: "Zeus, most glorious and greatest of the ever-living gods, take whichever of these your heart within you bids."

He spoke with deceit in mind. But Zeus, whose wisdom is everlasting, recognized and did not fail to perceive the trick; and he foresaw evil in his heart for mortal men, which was indeed to be fulfilled. With both hands he took up the white fat. Anger rose up within him and fury came upon his spirit when he saw the white bones of the ox laid out by cunning craft.

From that time forward, the tribes of men upon the earth burn white bones for the immortals upon smoking altars.

And Zeus, who thunders on high, was stung to his core, and his heart was filled with rage when he saw the far-shining ray of fire among men. Immediately he devised an evil thing for men in exchange for fire; for the renowned Limping God molded from earth the likeness of a shy maiden, as the son of Cronos desired. The goddess bright-eyed Athene dressed and adorned her in silvery clothing, and over her head Athene draped with her hands an embroidered veil, a marvel to behold; and Pallas Athene placed around her head lovely garlands, fresh-blooming flowers and herbs. On it was engraved intricate and wondrous work; for of the many creatures nurtured by land and sea, he had depicted most of them there — remarkable things, like living creatures with voices — and great beauty radiated from it.

But when he had fashioned this beautiful evil in place of a good, he brought her out where the other gods and men were, adorned with the finery of the grey-eyed daughter of a mighty father. Wonder seized the immortal gods and mortal men when they saw this sheer deception, irresistible to men. For from her comes the race of women who are female, and from her is the deadly race and tribe of women who live among mortal men to their great trouble, no help in hateful poverty, but only in wealth. And he granted yet another evil in place of good: whoever avoids marriage and the sorrows that women cause, and is unwilling to wed, reaches destructive old age without anyone to tend him; though he does not lack livelihood while he lives, when he is dead strangers divide his property among themselves. As for the man who does have the fortune to marry, if he gets a wife of suitable disposition, evil contends with good throughout his life continually; but whoever gets one of the harmful sort, he lives with an unceasing pain in his heart and spirit, and that is an incurable evil.

THE SHIELD OF HERACLES

She alone, leaving behind her home and native land,
came to Thebes following Amphitryon, the warrior,
Alcmene, daughter of Electryon, marshal of peoples.
She surpassed the race of womanly women
in beauty and in stature; and in mind none could rival her
among those whom mortal women bore, sleeping with mortal men.
From her head and from her dark eyelashes
breathed a fragrance like that of golden Aphrodite.
She honored her husband according to her own heart
as no woman among womanly women ever did;
for her noble father had been slain by him in rage
over cattle; and he, leaving his native land,
came as a suppliant to Thebes, to the shield-bearing Cadmeans.
There he dwelt in his house with his modest wife,
apart from the delights of love, for it was not permitted him
to mount the bed of Electryon's fair-ankled daughter
before he had avenged the death of her great-hearted brothers
and burned with raging fire the villages
of the heroic Taphians and Teleboans.
For so it was agreed between them, and the gods were witnesses;
and he feared their wrath, and pressed on to accomplish as quickly as possible
the great deed that heaven's justice required of him.
With him, eager for war and the din of battle,
the Boeotians, breakers of horses, breathing over their shields,
the Locrians, fighters at close range, and the great-hearted Phocians
followed; and the noble son of Alcaeus led them,
glorying among his people. And the father of men and gods—

He wove another plan in his mind, so as to beget for gods and men a defender against destruction. Setting out from Olympus with guile in his heart, longing for the love of a well-girded woman, he traveled by night; he came quickly to Typhaonion, and from there Zeus the counselor climbed to the very summit of Phikion. There, sitting down, he devised wondrous deeds in his mind. For on that very night he lay with Electryon's daughter of the slender ankles in love and desire, and fulfilled his wish; and on that same night Amphitryon, the rallier of peoples, the glorious hero, having accomplished his great task, came home to his house. He did not go to his slaves or his country shepherds before he had mounted his wife's bed — such was the longing that gripped the shepherd of the people. And as a man gladly escapes the misery of a painful illness or harsh imprisonment, so at that time Amphitryon, having rid himself of his hard toil, came joyfully and gladly to his own home. All night long he lay with his modest wife, delighting in the gifts of golden Aphrodite. She, having been mastered by a god and by a man who was far the best, bore twin children in seven-gated Thebes — children who did not share the same mind, though they were brothers: one the lesser, but the other by far the greater man, the dread and mighty strength of Heracles. The one she conceived by the dark-clouded son of Kronos, the other — Iphikles the spear-skilled — by Amphitryon: a divided lineage, the one conceived with a mortal man, the other with Zeus the son of Kronos, lord over all the gods.

This Battos lived on the top of the crag, and when he heard the lowing of the calves as they were driven past, he came out of his house and realized that the cattle were stolen. He asked for a reward in exchange for telling no one about them. Hermes promised to give it, and Battos swore to reveal the cattle to no one. When Hermes had hidden them in the cave on the headland opposite Italy and Sicily, by the Koryphasion promontory, he returned again to Battos, having changed his own appearance, to test whether he would hold to his oath.

"I am filled with wonder at the number of figs this wild fig-tree bears, small as it is. Can you tell me their number?"

How then shall I hymn you, who are in every way worthy of song? For everywhere, Phoebus, the realm of song is laid open to you, both over the mainland that nurtures cattle and over the islands. All the peaks please you, and the high headlands of lofty mountains, and the rivers flowing down to the sea, and the capes sloping toward the deep, and the harbors of the sea.

At once the immortals delight in lyre and song; the Muses all together, answering one another with beautiful voice, hymn the immortal gifts of the gods and the endurance of men — all that men suffer at the hands of the immortal gods, living witless and helpless, unable to find a cure for death or a defense against old age. So he spoke; and they listened to him well and obeyed.

They tried to bind him with heavy chains, but the bonds could not hold him, and the ropes fell away from his hands and feet; and he sat there with a smile in his dark eyes. Then the helmsman grasped what was happening and called out to his companions at once, saying:
"Fools! What god is this you have seized and are trying to bind, powerful as he is? Not even our stout ship can hold him. Surely this must be Zeus, or Apollo of the silver bow, or Poseidon, for he looks nothing like mortal men — he looks like the gods

¹ Probably not Etruscans, but the non-Hellenic peoples of Thrace and (according to Thucydides) of Lemnos and Athens. Cf. Herodotus i. 57; Thucydides iv. 109.

like the gods who hold the mansions of Olympus. Come, let us set him ashore on the dark mainland at once; do not lay hands on him, lest in his anger he stir up fierce winds and a great tempest against us."

So he spoke, but the captain rebuked him with a harsh word: "Fool, watch the wind and help haul the sail of the ship — take hold of all the tackle. This fellow will be our men's concern. I expect he will reach Egypt or Cyprus or the Hyperboreans or somewhere even farther; in the end he will tell us about his own friends and all his possessions and his brothers, since a god has thrown him into our hands."

So saying, he stepped the mast and drew up the sail of the ship. The wind filled the middle of the sail, and the crew stretched the tackle taut on either side; but soon wondrous deeds appeared before them. First, sweet-tasting wine began to gurgle pleasantly throughout the swift black ship, and an ambrosial fragrance arose; amazement seized all the sailors at the sight. Next, a vine spread out to the very top of the sail, hanging in clusters on either side, and dark ivy coiled around the mast, blooming with flowers, and lovely fruit appeared upon it; all the thole-pins were garlanded. When they saw this, they at last bade the helmsman steer the ship to land. But the god became a terrible lion in the interior of the ship, up at the bow, and roared aloud, and in the middle of the vessel he created a shaggy-necked bear, showing signs of his power; the bear reared up in fury, while the lion on the foredeck glared down with a terrible look. The crew fled in terror to the stern,

XXXI

TO HELIOS (THE SUN)

Begin now, O Muse, daughter of Zeus, to sing of Helios the radiant, whom ox-eyed Euryphaessa bore, child of Earth and starry Heaven. For Hyperion wed glorious Euryphaessa, his own sister, who bore him beautiful children: rosy-armed Eos, and lovely-haired Selene, and tireless Helios, like unto the immortals, who shines upon mortals and immortals alike, riding his horses. Terribly he gazes from beneath his golden helmet; bright rays blaze brilliantly from him, and his bright hair streams from his temples, framing his gracious and far-shining face. A beauty contest is stirred up among Athena, Hera, and Aphrodite, who are led by Hermes to Alexander on Mount Ida for judgment, in accordance with the command of Zeus; and Alexander, won over by the promise of Helen's hand in marriage, awards the prize to Aphrodite.

Then, at Aphrodite's suggestion, a fleet is built, and Helenus prophesies to him about what is to come. Aphrodite orders Aeneas to sail with him. And Cassandra reveals what is to come. Landing in Lacedaemon, Alexander is entertained by the Tyndaridae, and after that by Menelaus in Sparta; and during the feast Alexander gives gifts to Helen.

After this Menelaus sails off to Crete, having instructed Helen to provide the guests with everything they need until they depart. In the meantime Aphrodite brings Helen together with Alexander. After their union, they take on board most of the valuables and sail away by night. But Hera sends a storm against them. Alexander is driven to Sidon and captures the city. Then he sails to Ilion and celebrates his marriage with Helen.

Meanwhile Castor and Polydeuces are caught stealing the cattle of Idas and Lynceus; Castor is killed by Idas, and Lynceus and Idas are killed by Polydeuces. Zeus grants them immortality on alternate days.

After this Iris reports to Menelaus what has happened at his home. He returns and takes counsel with his brother about a campaign against Ilion, and goes to visit Nestor.

Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite competed over which of them is the most beautiful. The three were led by Hermes, at Zeus's command, to Alexandrus on Mount Ida for his judgment, and Alexandrus, enticed by the promise of marriage with Helen, decided in favor of Aphrodite.

Then Alexandrus built his ships at Aphrodite's suggestion, and Helenus foretold the future to him, and Aphrodite ordered Aeneas to sail with him, while Cassandra prophesied what would happen afterward. Alexandrus then landed in Lacedaemon and was entertained by the sons of Tyndareus, and afterward by Menelaus in Sparta, where during a feast he gave gifts to Helen.

After this, Menelaus set sail for Crete, ordering Helen to provide the guests with everything they needed until they departed. Meanwhile, Aphrodite brought Helen and Alexandrus together, and they, after their union, loaded a great treasure on board and sailed away by night. Hera stirred up a storm against them and they were driven to Sidon, where Alexandrus captured the city. From there he sailed to Troy and celebrated his marriage with Helen.

In the meantime, Castor and Polydeuces, while stealing the cattle of Idas and Lynceus, were caught in the act; Castor was killed by Idas, and Lynceus and Idas were killed by Polydeuces. Zeus granted them immortality on alternating days.

Iris then informed Menelaus of what had happened at his home. Menelaus returned and planned an expedition against Troy with his brother, and then went on

Then Telephus, following an oracle, comes to Argos and Achilles heals him, since he is to be their guide on the voyage to Ilium.

When the fleet had assembled for the second time at Aulis, Agamemnon, while hunting, shot a deer and boasted that he surpassed even Artemis. ...they attempt to sacrifice her. But Artemis snatches her away, transports her to the Taurians, and makes her immortal; in place of the girl she sets a deer at the altar.

Then they sail to Tenedos. While they are feasting there, Philoctetes is bitten by a water-snake and, on account of the stench of the wound, is left behind on Lemnos. Achilles, having been invited later, quarrels with Agamemnon. Then, as they attempt to land at Ilion, the Trojans drive them back, and Protesilaus is killed by Hector. After that Achilles turns them to flight by slaying Cycnus, the son of Poseidon. They recover their dead, and send ambassadors to the Trojans demanding the return of Helen and the treasure. When the Trojans refuse, they then assault the walls. Next they go out over the surrounding country and sack the neighboring cities. After this Achilles desires to see Helen, and Aphrodite and Thetis bring the two of them together. Then, when the Achaeans are eager to return home, Achilles holds them back. He then drives off the cattle of Aeneas, and sacks Lyrnessus and Pedasus and many of the neighboring cities, and kills Troilus. Patroclus takes Lycaon to Lemnos and sells him into slavery. From the spoils Achilles receives Briseis as his prize of honor, and Agamemnon receives Chryseis. Then follows the death of Palamedes, and the Plan of Zeus as to how he might relieve the Trojans by detaching Achilles from the Greek alliance, and a catalogue of those who fought as allies of the Trojans.

THE AETHIOPIS

1.

The Cypria, described in the preceding book, has its sequel in the Iliad of Homer, which is followed in turn by the five books of the Aethiopis, the work of Arctinus of Miletus. Their contents are as follows. The Amazon Penthesileia, daughter of Ares and of Thracian descent, comes to aid the Trojans, and after displaying great prowess, is killed by Achilles and buried by the Trojans. Achilles then slays Thersites for insulting and mocking him over his supposed love for Penthesileia. As a result, a dispute breaks out among the Achaeans over the killing of Thersites, and Achilles sails to Lesbos, where after sacrificing to Apollo, Artemis, and Leto, he is purified by Odysseus of the bloodshed.
Then Memnon, the son of Eos, wearing armor made by Hephaestus, comes to help the Trojans, and Thetis informs her son about Memnon. A battle takes place in which Antilochus is slain by Memnon and Memnon by Achilles. Eos then obtains from Zeus and bestows upon her son immortality; but Achilles routs the Trojans and, rushing into the city with

Next come two books of the Sack of Ilium, by Arctinus of Miletus, with the following contents. The Trojans were suspicious of the wooden horse and, standing around it, debated what they ought to do. THE TELEGONY

1.

After the Returns comes the Odyssey of Homer, and then the Telegony in two books by Eugammon of Cyrene, which contains the following material. The suitors of Penelope are buried by their kinsmen, and Odysseus, after making sacrifices to the Nymphs, sails to Elis to inspect his herds. He is entertained there by Polyxenus and receives a mixing bowl as a gift; the story of Trophonius, Agamedes, and Augeas then follows. He next sails back to Ithaca and carries out the sacrifices commanded by Teiresias, and then travels to Thesprotis where he marries Callidice, queen of the Thesprotians. A war then breaks out between the Thesprotians, led by Odysseus, and the Brygi. Ares routs the army of Odysseus, and Athena engages Ares, until Apollo separates them. After the death of Callidice, Polypoetes, the son of Odysseus, inherits the kingdom, while Odysseus himself returns to Ithaca. Meanwhile, Telegonus, while traveling in search of his father, lands on Ithaca and plunders the island. Odysseus comes out to defend his country but is killed by his own son, without either knowing who the other was. When Telegonus realizes his mistake, he brings his father's body along with Penelope and Telemachus to his mother's island, where Circe makes them immortal. Telegonus then marries Penelope, and Telemachus marries Circe.

Beginning, I pray that the chorus of the Muses come from Helicon into my heart for the sake of a song that I lately placed on my knees and wrote on my tablets — a boundless strife, a war-stirring work of Ares — praying that it reach the ears of all mortal men: how mice made themselves glorious in battle against the frogs, imitating the deeds of the earth-born Giants, as the tale was told among mortals. Such was its beginning.

Once a thirsty mouse, having escaped the danger of a weasel, drew his soft chin near a lake, delighting in the honey-sweet water. The loud-voiced Marsh-rejoicer caught sight of him and spoke these words: "Stranger, who are you? Where do you come from to this shore? Who is your father? Tell me everything truly; do not let me catch you in a lie. For if I find you to be a worthy friend, I will bring you to my home, and I will give you many fine gifts of hospitality. I am King Puffjaw, honored throughout the lake as leader of the frogs every day. My father Peleus raised me, having united in love with Hydromedusa by the banks of the Eridanus. I can see that you too are handsome and brave, outstanding above others, a scepter-bearing king and a warrior in battle. Come now, quickly tell your own lineage."

Everyone boasts that the most divine of poets, Homer and Hesiod, are said to be his particular countrymen. Hesiod, indeed, identified his birthplace and so put an end to any rivalry on the matter, for he said that his father "settled near Helicon in a wretched hamlet, Ascra, which is miserable in winter, sultry in summer, and good at no season." But as for Homer, one might almost say that every city and its inhabitants claims him as their own son. Foremost among them are the people of Smyrna, who say that he was the son of Meles, the river of their town, by a nymph named Cretheis, and that he was originally called Melesigenes. He was given the name Homer later, when he became blind, this being their customary epithet for such persons. The Chians, on the other hand, bring forward evidence to show that he was their countryman, saying that some of his descendants actually remain among them, who are called Homeridae. The Colophonians even point out the very spot where they claim he began to compose poetry while working as a schoolmaster, and say that his first work was the Margites.

For when the emperor inquired whence Homer came and who his parents were, she delivered the following response in hexameters:

You ask me of the lineage and native land

Telemachus is his father, and Nestor's daughter Epicaste

These verses deserve the greatest credence, both on account of the one who made the inquiry and the one who gave the answer, and especially since the poet has in this way gloriously celebrated his own ancestor through his verses.

Hearing this, he hesitated to go to Ios and stayed in the region where he was.
