CONTEST OF HOMER AND HESIOD

"Tell me this one thing I ask of you: how many Achaeans went with the sons of Atreus to Ilion?"

And he answers with a mathematical riddle:

"There were fifty hearth-fires, and at each fifty spits, and around each spit fifty pieces of meat; and three times three hundred Achaeans were gathered around each piece of meat."

This works out to an incredible number: for with fifty hearth-fires, there are two thousand five hundred spits, and one hundred and twenty myriads of pieces of meat....

Since Homer was getting the better of him in every way, Hesiod began again out of envy:

"O Homer of Meles, if indeed the Muses honor you — as the story goes, the daughters of great Zeus most high — fit your verse to measure and tell me what is most beautiful and what most hateful to mortals, for I long to hear."

And Homer replies:

"Hesiod, offspring of Zeus, you bid me speak these things willingly; and I will speak to you very gladly. The finest measure among good things is to be sufficient unto oneself; and the most hateful of all evils is the opposite. But ask me anything else that your heart desires."

"When the Pleiades, the daughters of Atlas, begin to rise, begin the harvest, and begin plowing before they set. Then Homer:

"The ranks stood firm around the two Aiantes, so steadfast that not even Ares would have scorned them had he met them, nor Athena who saves armies. There the chosen best waited for the charge of the Trojans and noble Hector, forming a wall of spears and massed shields. Shield pressed against shield, helmet against helmet, and man against man, and the crests of horsehair on their head-pieces touched as they leaned forward — so closely did they stand together. The murderous battle bristled with the long, flesh-rending spears they gripped, and the flash of bronze from polished helmets and freshly burnished breastplates and gleaming shields blinded the eyes. A man would have had to be very hard of heart to look upon that struggle with joy and feel no pain."

The Greeks, admiring Homer even in this, praised him, saying that the verses had been composed beyond what was fitting, and called for the victory to be given to him. But the king crowned Hesiod, declaring it just that the one who called men to farming and peace should win, not the one who described wars and slaughter. So they say Hesiod won the victory in this way, and taking a bronze tripod, dedicated it to the Muses, inscribing on it:

Hesiod dedicated this to the Heliconian Muses,
having defeated divine Homer in song at Chalcis.

When the contest was dissolved, Hesiod sailed to Delphi to consult the oracle and to dedicate first-fruits of his victory to the god. As he approached the temple, they say the prophetess, filled with divine inspiration, spoke:

Blessed is this man who tends my house,
Hesiod, honored by the immortal Muses;
his fame shall spread as far as the dawn extends.
But beware the beautiful grove of Nemean Zeus;
for there your fated end of death awaits you.

Hesiod, on hearing the oracle, withdrew from the Peloponnese, thinking the god meant the Nemea there. He went to Oenoe in Locris and lodged with Amphiphanes and Ganyctor, the sons of Phegeus, not recognizing the meaning of the oracle. For this entire region was called the sacred precinct of Nemean Zeus. After he had spent considerable time among the people of Oenoe, the young men, suspecting that Hesiod was seducing their sister, killed him—

CONTEST OF HOMER AND HESIOD

...sailing into the sea between Achaea and Locris, they threw him overboard. But on the third day the corpse was carried to shore by dolphins, during a local festival of the Ariadneia that was being held there. Everyone ran down to the beach, and recognizing the body, mourned for him and buried him, while they began searching for the murderers. The killers, fearing the anger of the citizens, seized a fishing boat and sailed away to Crete; but Zeus struck them with a thunderbolt in mid-voyage and drowned them, as Alcidamas says in his Mouseion. Eratosthenes, however, says in his work on Hesiod that Ctimenos and Antiphon, the sons of Ganyctor, for the aforementioned reason, were seized and sacrificed to the gods of hospitality by Eurycles the seer. But the maiden, the sister of the men just mentioned, after her violation hanged herself; she had been violated by a certain stranger who traveled with Hesiod, by name Demodous, and this man also was killed by the same people, he says. Later the Orchomenians, in accordance with an oracle, brought his remains and buried him among themselves, and inscribed upon the tomb:

Ascra was his birthplace, rich in grain, but in death

of Hesiod, whose glory is greatest among men

Entries include cross-references (indicated by dashes) and brief identifications, such as: Nereus, son of Sea, called the Old Man (p. 97); his daughters appear on pages 99, 153, 187, and 347.
